en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷamāluṅkyasutta, the sixty-third discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, while the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“These points of view which have been left undeclared by the Blessed One—set aside, rejected, and refused—namely:”

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’

‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ and ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—these the Blessed One does not explain to me.
Those things which the Blessed One does not explain to me do not please me; they are not acceptable to me.
Therefore, I shall approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter.
If the Blessed One explains to me:
“The world is eternal,” or “The world is not eternal,” and so forth...
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
for this purpose I shall lead the holy life under the Blessed One;
provided that the Blessed One does not explain it to me:
“Whether it be ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
having renounced such training, I shall return to the lower life.”
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘These points of view which have been left undeclared by the Blessed One, set aside, and rejected—namely:
“The world is eternal” and “The world is not eternal”… [and so on]…’”
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—the Blessed One does not explain these to me.
That which the Blessed One does not explain to me is not pleasing to me; that is not acceptable to me.
Therefore, having approached the Blessed One, I shall ask him about this matter.
If the Blessed One explains to me:
“The world is eternal,” or “The world is not eternal,” and so forth...
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
in this way, I shall lead the holy life under the Blessed One.
But if the Blessed One does not answer me:
‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’— thinking,
“I shall abandon this training and return to the lower life,” [one might commit such an offense].
If the Blessed One knows:
‘The world is eternal,’ let the Blessed One declare to me: ‘The world is eternal’; if the Blessed One knows: [‘the world is not eternal’]...
‘The world is eternal,’ let the Blessed One explain to me, ‘the world is eternal.

If the Blessed One does not know whether ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ then for one who does not know and does not see, it is simply straightforward to say this: [I do not know.]
‘I do not know, I do not see.

If the Blessed One knows that ‘the world is finite,’ let the Blessed One declare to me that ‘the world is finite’; if [he knows] that ‘the world is infinite,’ let the Blessed One declare to me that ‘the world is infinite.’
If the Blessed One knows:
‘The world is infinite,’ let the Blessed One declare to me: ‘The world is infinite.
If the Blessed One does not know:
Whether it be "the world is finite" or "the world is infinite," for one who does not know and does not see, this alone is straightforward:
namely, "I do not know, I do not see.
If the Blessed One knows:
‘That which is the soul is the body’—let the Blessed One explain to me: ‘That which is the soul is the body.
Or, if the Blessed One knows:
‘The soul is one thing, the body is another’—let the Blessed One explain to me: ‘The soul is one thing, the body is another.’

If the Blessed One does not know either "the soul is the same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another," then for one who does not know and does not see, it is simply straightforward to say:
"I do not know; I do not see."
If the Blessed One knows:
"The Tathāgata exists after death," let the Blessed One declare to me: "The Tathāgata exists after death"; if the Blessed One knows: [the Tathāgata does not exist after death...]
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’—let the Blessed One explain this to me.

If the Blessed One does not know whether ‘the Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ then for one who neither knows nor sees, it is simply straightforward to say this: [that he does not know].
‘I do not know, I do not see.
If the Blessed One knows that ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ let the Blessed One declare to me: ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’”
If the Blessed One knows:
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death," let the Blessed One declare to me: "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
If the Blessed One does not know:

“‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—for one who does not know and does not see, this alone is straightforward:
namely, ‘I do not know; I do not see.
“Māluṅkyaputta, did I ever say to you:”

"Come, Māluṅkyaputta, lead the holy life under me, and I will explain to you whether the world is eternal or whether the world is not eternal; whether the world is finite or whether the world is infinite;
whether the soul and the body are the same or whether the soul and the body are different; or whether the Tathāgata exists after death..."

“Or does he hold the view: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Or did you say this to me:
‘Venerable sir, I will lead the holy life under the Blessed One; the Blessed One will explain to me:
“the world is eternal,” or “the world is not eternal,” or “the world is finite,” or “the world is infinite”’?”

or “that the soul is the same as the body,” or “the soul is one thing and the body another,” or “a Tathāgata exists after death,” or “a Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death”?
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Māluṅkyaputta, it seems I did not say to you:
‘Come, Māluṅkyaputta, lead the holy life under me and I will explain this to you:’”
“Either ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’”; nor,
it seems, do you say this to me:
‘Venerable sir, I shall lead the holy life under the Blessed One; the Blessed One will explain to me:
“The world is eternal,” or “the world is not eternal”… [and so on] … or “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”’
This being so, foolish man, who are you, being yourself existent, that you reject another who is existent?
Māluṅkyaputta, if anyone were to say this:
“I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: [‘the world is eternal’] … [or] ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”
“Whether ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—
if that person were to die, Māluṅkyaputta, that would remain simply undeclared by the Tathāgata.”
"Just as if, Māluṅkyaputta, a man were pierced by an arrow thickly smeared with poison, and his friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives were to bring a physician or surgeon for him;
and he were to say: "
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know the man by whom I have been pierced—whether he be a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a suddo’;
or he might say:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know the man by whom I have been pierced, such that his name is so-and-so and his clan is so-and-so.’
He might say this:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know the man by whom I was pierced—whether he is tall, short, or of medium height’;
he might say this:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know the man by whom I was pierced—whether he is dark, or brown, or fair-skinned’;
or he might say:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know the man by whom I was pierced—in such-and-such a village, town, or city.’
He might say this:
“I will not extract this arrow until I know the bow by which I was pierced—whether it was a *cāpa* or a *kodaṇḍa*”;
he might further say this:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know whether it was made of horn, or of sinew, or of tendons, or of munja grass, or of balbaja grass, or of milk-wood’;
or he might say:
‘I will not extract this arrow until I know whether the shaft by which I am pierced was made of reed, or of cane, or of rushes, or of iron, or of wood. Thus he would speak.
He might say this:
“I will not extract this arrow until I know the shaft with which I was pierced—
whether it was fletched with the feathers of a vulture, or a heron, or a hawk, or a peacock.”
Or if he has a loose jaw, he might say:
“I will not extract this arrow until I know the shaft by which I have been pierced— whether it belongs to an ox, or a buffalo, or a bherava, or a semhāra, and with whose sinews it is bound.”
He might say this:
“I will not extract this arrow until I know by what I have been pierced—
whether it be a barb, or a pointed shaft, or a calf-toothed arrow, or an iron bolt, or a calf’s tooth.”
"Or suppose he were to say, 'Karavīrapattana'—
that too would be unknown to that man, Māluṅkyaputta, and then that man would die.
In the same way, Māluṅkyaputta, whoever should speak thus:"
‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me:
“The world is eternal,” or “The world is not eternal”… [and so on] …or “A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”’
“Māluṅkyaputta, that would have remained undeclared by the Tathāgata had that person died.
Māluṅkyaputta, if the view ‘the world is eternal’ were held, there would be a living of the holy life; this is not our position.
Māluṅkyaputta, if the view ‘the world is not eternal’ were held, there would be a living of the holy life; this also is not our position.”

“Māluṅkyaputta, when there is the view ‘the world is eternal’ or when there is the view ‘the world is not eternal,’ there is indeed birth, there is aging, there is death, and there are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, the destruction of which I prescribe here and now in this very life.
Māluṅkyaputta, if there were the view ‘the world is finite,’ would there be a living of the holy life? No, it would not.”
“Māluṅkyaputta, if there were the view ‘the world is infinite,’ there would still be living the holy life;

it is the same even if there were the view ‘the world is finite. Whether there is the view ‘the world is finite’ or the view ‘the world is infinite,’ Māluṅkyaputta, there is indeed birth, there is aging, there is death;
there are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, the destruction of which I prescribe here and now in this very life.”
“Māluṅkyaputta, if there were the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ there would be no living of the holy life; so it is for us.
If there were the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ there would be no living of the holy life; so it is for us as well.

Whether there be the view ‘the soul is the same as the body’ or the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ Māluṅkyaputta, there is still birth... [and so on]... suffering, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
I prescribe silence, Māluṅkyaputta.
If there were the view, "The Tathāgata exists after death," Māluṅkyaputta, the living of the holy life would not be possible; it is not so for us.
If there were the view, "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," Māluṅkyaputta, the living of the holy life would not be possible; it is also not so for us.
“Māluṅkyaputta, if there is the view ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or if there is the view ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ there is still birth...
[as before] ...for which I prescribe the destruction even here and now.
Māluṅkyaputta, if there is the view ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ would there be a living of the holy life? No, indeed.”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ Māluṅkyaputta—if such a view were held, there would be no living of the holy life; this too is so for us.

‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ Māluṅkyaputta—if such a view were held—or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—if such a view were held, there would still be birth...
[and so on] ...for which I prescribe the destruction even here and now.”
Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, remember what has been left undeclared by me as undeclared,
and remember what has been declared by me as declared.
And what, Māluṅkyaputta, has been left undeclared by me?
“‘The world is eternal,’ Māluṅkyaputta, has been left undeclared by me;
‘the world is not eternal’ has been left undeclared by me.”
‘The world is finite’—
this has not been declared by me; ‘the world is infinite’— this has not been declared by me.
I have not declared:
"That which is the soul is the same as the body";
I have not declared that.
‘The soul is one thing and the body another’—
this has not been declared by me;
‘the Tathāgata exists after death’— this has not been declared by me.
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’— this has been left undeclared by me; ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’—
this has been left undeclared by me.
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’—
this has not been declared by me;
‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’— this has not been declared by me.
I have left it undeclared.
And why, Māluṅkyaputta, have I left it undeclared?

Because this, Māluṅkyaputta, is not connected with the goal, not fundamental to the holy life, and does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
Therefore, that has been left undeclared by me.
And what, Māluṅkyaputta, has been declared by me?
"This is suffering," Māluṅkyaputta, has been declared by me.
"This is the origin of suffering"—
this has been declared by me; "This is the cessation of suffering"— this has been declared by me.
I have declared:
‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—
this I have declared.
And why, Māluṅkyaputta, have I declared this?

Because this, Māluṅkyaputta, is beneficial, this pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life; it leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Therefore, I have declared it.
"Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, remember what I have left undeclared as undeclared,
and remember what I have declared as declared.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Māluṅkyaputta was uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Cūḷamālukyasutta, the third, is finished.
